"L'amour est bleu" ({{IPA|fr|lamuʁ ɛ blø}}; "Love Is Blue") is a song recorded by Greek singer Vicky Leandros with music composed by André Popp and French lyrics written by Pierre Cour. It {{esccnty|Luxembourg|y=1967|t=represented Luxembourg}} in the Eurovision Song Contest 1967 held in Vienna, placing fourth.

It has since been recorded by many other musicians, most notably French orchestra leader Paul Mauriat, whose familiar instrumental version – recorded in late 1967 – became the first number-one by a French lead artist to top the Billboard Hot 100 in the United States.

sections.heading: Conception
sections.wikitext: "L'amour est bleu" was composed by [[André Popp]] with French lyrics by [[Pierre Cour]]. It describes the pleasure and pain of love in terms of colours (blue and grey) and elements (water and wind). The lyrics of the English version ("Blue, blue, my world is blue …") focus on colours only (blue, grey, red, green, and black), using them to describe components of lost love.<ref name="DG">{{Cite web|title="L'amour est bleu" - lyrics|url=http://www.diggiloo.net/?1967lu|website=The Diggiloo Thrush}}</ref>

sections.heading: Eurovision
sections.wikitext:
The {{lang|fr|[[Compagnie Luxembourgeoise de Télédiffusion]]|i=unset}} (CLT) internally selected "L'amour est bleu" as {{esccnty|Luxembourg|t=its entry}} for the {{escyr|1967||12th edition}} of the [[Eurovision Song Contest]], and a Greek-born 17-year-old [[Vicky Leandros]], as ''Vicky''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://eurovisionworld.com/national/1967|title=National Selections: 1967|website=Eurovisionworld}}</ref>

In addition to the French-language original version, she recorded the song in English –as "Colours of Love" with lyrics by Bryan Blackburn<!--- not the Australian gymnast from the 1950s --->–,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thestage.co.uk/obituaries--archive/obituaries/bryan-blackburn/|title=Bryan Blackburn - Obituary|work=The Stage}}</ref> German –as "Blau wie das Meer" with lyrics by Klaus Munro–, Italian –as "L'amore è blu"–, and Dutch –as "Liefde is zacht"–,<ref name="DG"/> that were released in nineteen countries.<ref>{{cite magazine |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=6ycEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA54 |title= Phillips releases Eurovision tune |magazine=Billboard |date=20 May 1967 |page=54}}</ref><ref name=mauriat>{{cite magazine |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=3g4EAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA48-IA3|title= Mauriat in America: A Surprise Single Prove Instrumental to His Success|first=Fred |last=Bronson |magazine=Billboard |date=20 January 1996 |page=P3}}</ref>

On 8 April 1967, the Eurovision Song Contest was held at the {{lang|de|[[Hofburg#Festival Hall Wing|Großer Festsaal der Wiener Hofburg]]|i=unset}} in [[Vienna]] hosted by {{lang|de|[[ORF (broadcaster)|Österreichischer Rundfunk]]|i=unset}} (ORF), and broadcast live throughout the continent. Vicky performed "L'amour est bleu" as the second song of the evening. Claude Denjean conducted the event's live orchestra in the performance of the entry.<ref>{{Cite episode|title=Eurovision Song Contest 1967|episode-link=Eurovision Song Contest 1967|series=Eurovision Song Contest|series-link=Eurovision Song Contest|network=[[ORF (broadcaster)|ORF]] / [[EBU]]|date=8 April 1967}}</ref>

At the close of voting, It had received 17 points, placing it fourth in a field of seventeen, behind "[[Il doit faire beau là-bas]]" (France), "[[If I Could Choose]]" (Ireland) and the winning song, "[[Puppet on a String (Sandie Shaw song)|Puppet on a String]]" (United Kingdom).<ref>{{cite book |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=XNbOAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA42|title= The Complete & Independent Guide to the Eurovision Song Contest 2012|first= Simon|last= Barclay |date= 2012|page=42|publisher= Lulu.com|isbn= 9781471756696}}</ref> It was succeeded as Luxembourgian representative at the {{escyr|1968||1968 contest}} by "[[Nous vivrons d'amour]]" by Chris Baldo & Sophie Garel.

In addition to the French-language original version, she recorded the song in English –as "Colours of Love" with lyrics by Bryan Blackburn–, German –as "Blau wie das Meer" with lyrics by Klaus Munro–, Italian –as "L'amore è blu"–, and Dutch –as "Liefde is zacht"–, that were released in nineteen countries.

On 8 April 1967, the Eurovision Song Contest was held at the {{lang|de|Großer Festsaal der Wiener Hofburg|i=unset}} in Vienna hosted by {{lang|de|Österreichischer Rundfunk|i=unset}} (ORF), and broadcast live throughout the continent. Vicky performed "L'amour est bleu" as the second song of the evening. Claude Denjean conducted the event's live orchestra in the performance of the entry.

At the close of voting, It had received 17 points, placing it fourth in a field of seventeen, behind "Il doit faire beau là-bas" (France), "If I Could Choose" (Ireland) and the winning song, "Puppet on a String" (United Kingdom). It was succeeded as Luxembourgian representative at the {{escyr|1968||1968 contest}} by "Nous vivrons d'amour" by Chris Baldo & Sophie Garel.

sections.heading: Aftermath
sections.wikitext:
Vicky Leandros went on to win Eurovision five years later with the song "[[Après toi]]", again representing Luxembourg.

"L'amour est bleu" achieved greater success through cover versions of the song by other artists. Some forty years after its original release, "L'amour est bleu", along with [[Domenico Modugno]]'s "[[Nel blu, dipinto di blu (song)|Nel blu dipinto di blu]]" (better known as "Volare") and [[Mocedades]]' "[[Eres tú]]", still counts as one of very few non-winning Eurovision entries ever to become a worldwide hit. The song has since become a favourite of Contest fans, most notably appearing as part of a medley introducing the semi-final of the [[Eurovision Song Contest 2006]] in [[Athens]], one of only three non-winning songs to be involved (the others being "[[Dschinghis Khan (song)|Dschinghis Khan]]" and "Nel blu dipinto di blu").

In 2026, Vicky Leandros returned to Eurovision to perform "L'amour est bleu" at the opening of the first semi-final as part of celebrations marking the 70th contest. Vicky's performance was the culmination of a montage of past Eurovision moments as viewed by a man called Tony who was seen (portrayed by multiple actors) as a boy as the 1950s Eurovision moments played out, and was then seen moving through the various stages of his life as the moments from the contest being played moved through the decades and showed the contest moving through different stages of its own existence.

According to [[Paul Mauriat]], who conducted/recorded an orchestral "[[easy listening]]" version of "Love Is Blue", he chose the song because it was published by his label, [[Philips Records]], even though he was not fond of the song. A DJ in [[Minneapolis]] played the recording and asked the audience to respond, and was inundated with phone calls about the song, and interest in the song then quickly spread around the country.<ref name=legrand /> 

The song became a [[Hot 100 number-one hits of 1968 (USA)|number-one hit in the USA]] for five weeks in February and March 1968, the first recording by a French artist to top the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]]. (It remained the only French song to top the chart until 2017, when [[Daft Punk]] was a featured artist on [[Canadians|Canadian]] artist [[The Weeknd]]'s number-one hit "[[Starboy (song)|Starboy]]".)  Mauriat's version became a [[Music recording sales certification|gold record]], and its five-week run at the top is the second longest of any instrumental of the Hot 100 era, after "[[Theme from A Summer Place|Theme from ''A Summer Place'']]". The song also spent 11 weeks atop ''Billboard's'' Easy Listening survey, and held the longest-lasting title honours on this chart for 25 years. ''Billboard'' ranked the record as the No. 2 song for [[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1968|1968]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bobborst.com/popculture/songoftheyear/|title=Number One Song of the Year: 1946–2015|work=Bob Borst's Home of Pop Culture|access-date=3 November 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180420175438/http://www.bobborst.com/popculture/songoftheyear/|archive-date=20 April 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> It is the best-known version of the song in the United States. The Mauriat recording also reached No. 2 in Canada<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/obj/028020/f2/nlc008388.100175.pdf| title=RPM Top 100 Singles - March 2, 1968}}</ref> (No. 12 Year End),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/obj/028020/f2/nlc008388.5867.pdf| title=RPM Top 100 of 1968 - January 6, 1969}}</ref> and No. 12 on the [[UK Singles Chart]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.officialcharts.com/search/singles/love-is-blue-(l'amour-est-bleu)/|title=Love is blue (L'amour est bleu) | full Official Chart History | Official Charts Company|website=[[Official Charts Company|Official Charts]] }}</ref> The Mauriat album containing "Love Is Blue", ''[[Blooming Hits]]'', also reached No. 1 on the Billboard Top LP's and Tapes chart for five weeks. The song sold fewer than 30,000 units in France, but 2 million singles and 800,000 LPs were sold in the US.<ref name=legrand>{{cite magazine |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=3g4EAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA48-IA5|title= Paul Mauriat: The Interview |magazine=Billboard |date=20 January 1996 |pages=P3–5|first=Emmanuel |last=Legrand}}</ref>

According to Paul Mauriat, who conducted/recorded an orchestral "easy listening" version of "Love Is Blue", he chose the song because it was published by his label, Philips Records, even though he was not fond of the song. A DJ in Minneapolis played the recording and asked the audience to respond, and was inundated with phone calls about the song, and interest in the song then quickly spread around the country. 

The song became a number-one hit in the USA for five weeks in February and March 1968, the first recording by a French artist to top the Billboard Hot 100. (It remained the only French song to top the chart until 2017, when Daft Punk was a featured artist on Canadian artist The Weeknd's number-one hit "Starboy".)  Mauriat's version became a gold record, and its five-week run at the top is the second longest of any instrumental of the Hot 100 era, after "Theme from A Summer Place". The song also spent 11 weeks atop Billboard's Easy Listening survey, and held the longest-lasting title honours on this chart for 25 years. Billboard ranked the record as the No. 2 song for 1968. It is the best-known version of the song in the United States. The Mauriat recording also reached No. 2 in Canada (No. 12 Year End), and No. 12 on the UK Singles Chart. The Mauriat album containing "Love Is Blue", Blooming Hits, also reached No. 1 on the Billboard Top LP's and Tapes chart for five weeks. The song sold fewer than 30,000 units in France, but 2 million singles and 800,000 LPs were sold in the US.

*Mauriat's version was featured repeatedly in an episode of [[Chris Carter (screenwriter)|Chris Carter]]'s television series ''[[Millennium (TV series)|Millennium]]'' titled "[[A Room with No View]]", which originally aired on 24 April 1998 on the [[Fox Broadcasting Company|Fox Network]]. During the episode, the omnipresent melody is used by a kidnapper to [[brainwashing|brainwash]] a group of youths.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://millennium-thisiswhoweare.net/cmeacg/millennium_episode_music.php?id=40&mlm_code=220|title=Paul Mauriat – A Room With No View – Millennium Episode Music|work=millennium-thisiswhoweare.net|access-date=7 May 2008|archive-date=13 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161113070343/http://millennium-thisiswhoweare.net/cmeacg/millennium_episode_music.php?id=40&mlm_code=220|url-status=dead}}</ref>

sections.heading: Other covers
sections.wikitext:
* Three other recordings of the song charted on ''Billboard'' Hot 100 together with Paul Mauriat's version at the same time in 1968. [[Al Martino]]'s "Love is Blue" peaked at No. 57 on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] and No. 3 on the [[Hot Adult Contemporary Tracks|Billboard Adult Contemporary]] charts, and was the title song of one of his 1968 albums.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.allmusic.com/artist/al-martino-mn0000509367/awards|title=Al Martino|author=Steve Huey|work=AllMusic}}</ref> [[Claudine Longet]]'s "Love Is Blue (L'amour est bleu)" peaked at No. 71,<ref>[http://www.allmusic.com/artist/claudine-longet-mn0000145218/awards Claudine Longet: Awards], AllMusic</ref> while Manny Kellem's version reached No. 100.<ref name=mauriat />
* [[Jeff Beck]] recorded a [[Rock music|rock]] interpretation of Mauriat's version in 1968. It reached No. 20 in Ireland,<ref name=ireland /> and No. 23 on the [[UK Singles Chart]].<ref>[http://www.officialcharts.com/artist/12927/JEFF%20BECK/ Jeff Beck: Singles], [[Official Charts Company]]</ref>
* [[The Dells]] recorded a [[Soul music|soul]] medley, "[[I Can Sing a Rainbow]]/Love Is Blue", which reached No. 22 in the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 5 in the [[Billboard R&B Singles]] charts in the US, No. 10 in the Dutch chart,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://dutchcharts.nl/showitem.asp?interpret=The+Dells&titel=I+Can+Sing+A+Rainbow+%2F+Love+Is+Blue&cat=s|title=The Dells - I Can Sing A Rainbow / Love is Blue |work=Dutch Charts }}</ref> No. 18 in Ireland,<ref name=ireland /> and No. 16 in the UK charts, in 1969.<ref>[http://www.allmusic.com/artist/the-dells-mn0000147200/awards The Dells: Awards], AllMusic</ref><ref>[http://www.officialcharts.com/artist/13713/THE-DELLS/ Dells: Singles], [[Official Charts Company]]</ref>
sections.text:
* Three other recordings of the song charted on Billboard Hot 100 together with Paul Mauriat's version at the same time in 1968. Al Martino's "Love is Blue" peaked at No. 57 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 3 on the Billboard Adult Contemporary charts, and was the title song of one of his 1968 albums. Claudine Longet's "Love Is Blue (L'amour est bleu)" peaked at No. 71, while Manny Kellem's version reached No. 100.
* Jeff Beck recorded a rock interpretation of Mauriat's version in 1968. It reached No. 20 in Ireland, and No. 23 on the UK Singles Chart.
* The Dells recorded a soul medley, "I Can Sing a Rainbow/Love Is Blue", which reached No. 22 in the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 5 in the Billboard R&B Singles charts in the US, No. 10 in the Dutch chart, No. 18 in Ireland, and No. 16 in the UK charts, in 1969.
